I now have very comprehensive information. Let me check the Hoover Institution's "Proposition Lab" analysis, and if possible the Berkeley IGS guide, for a more balanced perspective, and then reach a conclusion.

Key points so far:

**Arguments in favor:**
1. Accountability/transparency: clinics must publicly report how they spend money (mission spending ratio published by the Attorney General).
2. Reduces wasteful executive pay/administrative costs; ensures dollars are directed toward patient care.
3. SEIU-UHW's argument: given federal funding cuts, every dollar matters.
4. The "90%" number is not arbitrary: FQHCs are already subject to a federal rule requiring 90% of HRSA grant funds to be spent on program services — but this measure extends that standard to all revenue.
5. Penalty is refundable if compliant within 5 years.

**Arguments against (stronger on the evidence):**
1. Clinics currently spend an average of only about 80% on healthcare services (per nonpartisan LAO); BRG analysis (commissioned by CPCA, though it's an independent research firm) found that 89–91% of clinic organizations would fail in year one, with approximately $1.6–1.7 billion in penalties in year one, with up to 88% of clinics operating at a loss.
2. The text is vague: "program services that further charitable purposes" is undefined; the Attorney General will determine what counts — significant uncertainty.
3. Risk that clinics will be forced to close (several hundred), reducing services for approximately 7 million patients in underserved communities.
4. Opposed by an overwhelming coalition: California Medical Association, AAP CA, CA Academy of Family Physicians, California Primary Care Association (the industry association for these clinics), California Hospital Association, Association of California Healthcare Districts, California Teachers Association, Planned Parenthood California, State Democratic Party, State Chamber of Commerce, Reform California, local boards of supervisors and chambers of commerce. No major medical organizations are in favor.
5. Political motive: SEIU-UHW's history of failed ballot measures related to dialysis (lost 2018, 2020, 2022 — a 0-3 record), allegedly used as leverage in organizing; CPCA filed a racketeering lawsuit alleging the initiative was designed to extract concessions.
6. Polling: 34% support (PPIC), the least popular of the measures surveyed.
7. Funding: approximately $38.6 million for No vs. approximately $16.9 million for Yes.
8. Editorials: all major ones I've found recommend No (McClatchy/Sacramento Bee, Press Democrat, Mercury News/East Bay Times, San Diego Union-Tribune, LA Daily News, Santa Cruz Sentinel, San Luis Obispo Tribune). I haven't found any major Yes editorials.
9. Existing oversight: FQHCs already report annually to federal and state governments; HRSA has compliance requirements; the measure adds state enforcement bureaucracy costing $10 million+ annually, paid for by the clinics themselves.

To balance things out, let me quickly check the Hoover Institution's analysis and the Berkeley IGS guide. Also, let me check if there are any prominent Yes endorsements I've missed.

California Decides (https://cms.hoover.org/publications/california-decides)
Quick Facts
Official ballot title: “Requires Community Health Clinics Spend 90% of Revenue on Program Services. Initiative Statute” (circulating title and summary issued by the attorney general, October 7, 2025). The measure’s own name is the “Clinic Funding Accountability and Transparency Act.”
Type: Initiated state statute (AG No. 25-0008A1). It adds new sections to the Government Code and the Health and Safety Code. It is not a constitutional amendment.
A vote YES means: Nonprofit federally qualified health centers must spend at least 90 percent of their total annual revenue on mission-related “program services” or pay a penalty equal to the shortfall. Clinics must report the underlying figures to the attorney general, who publishes a “mission spend ratio” for each clinic.
A vote NO means: No revenue-spending floor is imposed on these clinics. Their spending stays governed by existing nonprofit and federal-grant rules and by their own boards.
Sponsor/proponent: Californians for Responsible Healthcare, sponsored by SEIU-UHW West (Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West). Proponents of record are Shawna Brown and Sean Fleming.
On the ballot because: Proponents submitted about 1.03 million signatures on April 1, 2026, against a 546,651 valid signature requirement, and the secretary of state projected enough valid signatures to qualify for the November 3, 2026, ballot.
Full legal text: Initiative 25-0008A1, “Clinic Funding Accountability and Transparency Act,” California Office of the Attorney General (PDF) (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0008A1%20%28%26quot%3BClinic%20Funding%20Accountability%20and%20Transparency%20Act%26quot%3B%29.pdf)
LAO analysis: Ballot analysis of Initiative 2025-008 (https://www.lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Initiative/2025-008)
1. What would it do?
Proposition 44 would set a spending floor on California’s nonprofit community health clinics. Each covered clinic would have to spend at least 90 percent of its total annual revenue on “program services” that advance its charitable mission, meaning patient care and related services rather than management, overhead, or accumulated surplus [1, Sec. 3].
The measure works through a ratio it calls the mission spend ratio. That ratio is the amount a clinic spends on activities accomplishing its exempt purpose divided by its total revenue [1, Sec. 3]. The building blocks come from the clinic’s IRS Form 990. The numerator starts from “total program service expenses” on line 4e of Part III, and the denominator starts from total revenue on line 12 of Part I, for tax year 2024 or later [1, Sec. 3(b)(1)]. The attorney general may issue binding guidance adjusting how both figures are counted, so the final definition of qualifying spending is not fixed in the text—it is delegated [1, Sec. 3(b)(2)].
A clinic whose mission spend ratio falls below 90 percent would owe an administrative penalty equal to the gap between what it actually spent on mission-directed expenses and 90 percent of its total revenue [1, Sec. 4(b)(1)]. Penalty money is held in escrow in a state fund for five years. A clinic can get the money back if it comes into compliance and agrees with the Department of Public Health on a plan to spend the returned funds on mission-directed expenses. Money not returned within five years is appropriated for clinic-worker training, recruitment, and retention [1, Sec. 4(a)]. The Department of Public Health can grant one-year waivers for unexpected or exceptional circumstances or where compliance would raise going-concern doubts under generally accepted accounting principles [1, Sec. 4(c)]. Separate reporting fines of $5,000 for a first violation and $10,000 per month thereafter apply to clinics that do not file on time [1, Sec. 3(d)].
2. The legal language
Full text: Initiative 25-0008A1, “Clinic Funding Accountability and Transparency Act” (as amended September 2025), California Office of the Attorney General (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0008A1%20%28%26quot%3BClinic%20Funding%20Accountability%20and%20Transparency%20Act%26quot%3B%29.pdf)
Key language:
“‘Mission Spend Ratio’ is the total amount spent on activities that accomplish each clinic’s exempt purpose divided by that clinic’s total revenue.” [1, Sec. 3(a)(2)]
“The Department of Public Health shall annually assess on each clinic subject to Section 12586.3 of the Government Code that has a Mission Spend Ratio below ninety percent (90%) an administrative penalty equal to the difference between the amount the clinic spent on mission-directed expenses and 90 percent of the clinic’s total revenue.” [1, Sec. 4(b)(1)]
What it amends: Adds Section 12586.3 to the Government Code (reporting and the mission spend ratio) and Section 1234.1 to the Health and Safety Code (penalties and the escrow fund) [1, Secs. 3-4]. As an initiative statute rather than a constitutional amendment, the legislature could later amend it only in ways consistent with the measure’s terms.
3. What, Where, When, Why?
Who? The covered universe is narrow. A “clinic” under the measure means a nonprofit clinic corporation that is a federally qualified health center (FQHC) under federal law, and it expressly includes “FQHC Look-Alikes,” which meet FQHC program requirements without receiving the federal grant [1, Sec. 3(a)(1)]. The measure excludes federally recognized tribes, tribal organizations, and urban Indian organizations [1, Sec. 3(a)(1)]. It does not reach hospitals, for-profit clinics, or medical groups. The sponsor is SEIU-UHW West, a union representing roughly 120,000 healthcare workers, through the committee Californians for Responsible Healthcare. The opposition is led by the California Primary Care Association and allied clinics, operating as Protect Patients California.
What? A hard floor requiring at least 90 percent of total revenue to go to program services, enforced by a penalty equal to the shortfall, plus annual reporting and a state-published mission spend ratio for every covered clinic [1, Secs. 3-4].
Where? Statewide, applied to every nonprofit FQHC and FQHC Look-Alike operating in California.
When? On the November 3, 2026, ballot. The mission spend ratio calculation is built on Form 990 data for tax year 2024 or later, and the attorney general must make each clinic’s data public within ninety days of receipt [1, Sec. 3(b)(4)].
Why? The proponents’ findings say many clinics spend excessive shares of revenue on executive compensation and administration, that some report surpluses as high as 20 percent of revenue, and that clinic workers face chronic understaffing and turnover. The stated intent is to create “a reasonable minimum standard of mission-directed spending” so that patient care and workforce stability are prioritized over management and overhead [1, Sec. 2].
4. Trade-offs
Proposition 44 is one front in a long-running fight between SEIU-UHW and the California healthcare industry. The union placed three measures in this cycle: this clinic-spending floor, an executive-pay cap on hospitals and medical groups, and a billionaire wealth tax. The hospital industry answered with its own initiative requiring unions to get member approval before large political spending. Union-backed healthcare measures in California have a track record of functioning as leverage in labor-management disputes, most visibly the dialysis fights of 2018 through 2020, where roughly $340 million was spent and every measure failed. Reading Proposition 44 only as a patient-care reform, and not also as a bargaining instrument, misses half of what it is.
That does not make the underlying concern fake. FQHCs are nonprofit, tax-exempt, and heavily taxpayer funded. There is no serious dispute that some accumulate large surpluses or pay executives generously while frontline staffing lags. Requiring that a defined, high share of revenue flows to program services, while publishing each clinic’s ratio, is a coherent accountability idea with real appeal. The patient-care-first framing is not a pretext for nothing.
The hard question is whether a rigid revenue ratio is the right tool. Three features cut against it. First, the denominator is total revenue, not expenses. A clinic that runs a prudent operating surplus or builds reserves for a lean year is mechanically pushed below 90 percent and penalized, even if every dollar it spends is spent well. The measure effectively caps nonprogram spending plus surplus plus reserves at a combined 10 percent of revenue. Second, “program services” is anchored to a single Form 990 line, and the opposition argues that essential functions such as interpretation, transportation, and case management may not count, so clinics could be penalized for spending that patients experience as care. Third, the definition is not actually fixed. The attorney general may issue binding guidance moving the line in either direction, which concentrates significant discretion over clinic finances in one elected office [1, Sec. 3(b)(2)].
The measure tries to soften the edges with waivers for going-concern risk and for rural or distressed clinics, with a five-year window to earn penalties back [1, Sec. 4]. Whether those valves are wide enough is the crux. An opposition analysis commissioned by the clinics estimated that more than 90 percent of clinic organizations would face penalties totaling about $1.7 billion in the first year. That figure comes from an interested party and should be treated as a claim, not a finding, but even a fraction of it would fall on the safety-net providers that serve California’s lowest-income patients at the same moment federal Medicaid reductions are tightening their budgets.
5. Potential risks and benefits
Potential benefits
Proposition 44 creates a clear, published accountability metric for nonprofit clinics that receive large amounts of public money, letting the state and the public see how much of each clinic’s revenue reaches program services [1, Sec. 3(b)(4)].
It targets a real pattern the proponents document, in which some clinics report administrative costs of 30 to 40 percent of revenue or surpluses near 20 percent while frontline staffing suffers [1, Sec. 2].
Recovered penalties are steered toward clinic-worker training, recruitment, and retention, which addresses the understaffing the findings describe [1, Sec. 4(a)].
The escrow-and-refund design means a clinic that corrects course can recover its penalty rather than simply losing the money [1, Sec. 4(a)].
Waiver provisions for going-concern risk and for small, rural, or frontier clinics give the Department of Public Health room to protect the most vulnerable providers [1, Sec. 4(c)].
Potential risks
The floor is measured against total revenue, so a clinic can be penalized for running a prudent surplus or building reserves even when its actual spending is sound [1, Sec. 4(b)(1)].
Anchoring “program services” to one Form 990 line may exclude services patients rely on, such as interpretation, transportation, and case management, penalizing spending that functions as care.
The measure hands the attorney general broad discretion to redefine the numerator and denominator through binding guidance, concentrating power over clinic finances in an elected partisan office [1, Sec. 3(b)(2)].
It applies only to nonprofit FQHCs and Look-Alikes, the core of the safety net, and not to hospitals or for-profit providers, so the burden lands on the clinics serving the lowest-income patients [1, Sec. 3(a)(1)].
Penalties could reach from the hundreds of millions to more than a billion dollars in the first year on the opposition’s estimate, arriving alongside federal Medicaid cuts that are already straining clinic budgets.
The California Primary Care Association has a pending federal lawsuit arguing the measure conflicts with federal law governing FQHCs, so passage may not settle whether it can take effect.
The Legislative Analyst estimates state enforcement costs in the low tens of millions of dollars annually, partly offset by fees and penalties on the clinics themselves.
6. Open questions
How will the attorney general define “program services,” and will functions such as interpretation, transportation, and case management count toward the 90 percent?
Because the floor is measured against revenue, how will clinics that need operating surpluses or reserves avoid penalties without cutting into their financial cushion?
How many of California’s roughly 1,300-plus FQHC sites would actually fall below 90 percent under the final definition, and what is the realistic total penalty exposure once waivers are applied?
Will the Department of Public Health’s waiver process move fast enough to keep a distressed or rural clinic open before a penalty forces service cuts?
Does the measure conflict with federal FQHC funding and reimbursement rules, and how will the pending federal lawsuit resolve that before it can take effect?
Is a ballot-locked revenue ratio the right instrument for a problem that varies clinic by clinic, or would board-level and grant-level oversight fit better?
7. The questions to ask before you vote
“Spend 90 percent on patient care” sounds like a floor no one could oppose. But the measure counts spending against total revenue, ties “care” to one tax-form line the attorney general can redefine, and applies only to the nonprofit clinics that serve California’s poorest patients. Before you vote, ask whether this rewards clinics that spend well or mainly penalizes clinics that keep a surplus.
This measure sits inside a labor-industry fight, sponsored and fully funded by one union that has three measures on this ballot. Ask whether Proposition 44 would mostly change how safety-net clinics deliver care, or how much leverage one side carries into its next dispute with the healthcare industry.

Now I have a truly comprehensive overall picture. Let me weigh everything.

**What Proposition 44 does (November 3, 2026, California):**
- Requires private nonprofit Federally Qualified Health Centers (FQHCs) and FQHC Look-Alikes (about 2,000 safety-net clinics in California) to spend at least 90% of total annual revenue on "program services advancing charitable purposes."
- Administrative costs + overhead + surplus + reserves must total 10% or less of revenue (penalized against revenue, not expenditures).
- Penalty = the shortfall amount, held in escrow, refundable if the clinic comes into compliance within 5 years, otherwise the state keeps it and uses it for clinic worker training.
- The Attorney General defines the counting method (based on IRS Form 990 lines) and can issue binding guidance; the ratio is made public for each clinic.
- CDPH (California Department of Public Health) can waive in exceptional circumstances (one-year waiver).
- Criminal penalties for misreporting.
- Enforcement cost: $10 million or more per year, paid for by fees on clinics.
- Currently, clinics spend about 80% of revenue on healthcare services on average (LAO, nonpartisan).

**Strengths of the "No" case:**
1. Design flaws: The ratio is set against total revenue, not expenditures—clinics that build prudent reserves or run a small surplus will be penalized mechanically even if spending is efficient. Also, "program services" is anchored to a single Form 990 line, and important care-related costs (equipment, interpretation, transportation, case management, capital investments such as mammography equipment) may not count.
2. Scale of impact: An independent (but commissioned by CPCA) BRG analysis: 89–91% of clinic organizations fail in year one; approximately $1.6–1.7 billion (up to $1.9 billion) in first-year penalties; up to 88% of clinics in the red. Risk that hundreds of clinics will be forced to cut services or close—threatening about 7 million patients in underserved areas, precisely the safety net most in need of protection.
3. Ambiguity/discretion: The Attorney General—an elected partisan office—holds broad authority to redefine what counts; legal uncertainty for clinics.
4. Political context: SEIU-UHW's track record of 0-for-3 on similar dialysis measures (2018/2020/2022, roughly $340 million spent, all defeated), which critics say was used as unionization leverage. CPCA and five clinics filed a federal lawsuit alleging racketeering. The measure functions as a bargaining chip in labor disputes.
5. Overwhelming opposition from nearly all medical and clinic-related organizations: CA Medical Association, American Academy of Pediatrics (California Chapter), CA Academy of Family Physicians, American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists District IX, California Primary Care Association, California Hospital Association, Association of California Healthcare Districts, California Teachers Association, Planned Parenthood California, California State Democratic Party, California State Chamber of Commerce, Reform California, local boards of supervisors, chambers of commerce. On the other hand, no major medical organizations support it (only SEIU-UHW and the "Yes on 44" committee; the voter guide lists "Supporters: None submitted" for the argument).
6. Polls: 34% support—least popular of the 14 measures (PPIC).
7. Funding: $38.6 million "No" vs. $16.9 million "Yes."
8. Editorial consensus: All major editorial boards I found (McClatchy/Sacramento Bee, Merced, Modesto, Fresno, SLO, Press Democrat, Mercury News/East Bay Times, San Diego Union-Tribune, LA Daily News, Pasadena Star-News, Santa Cruz Sentinel, Bay Area Reporter, Daily Cal) recommend "No." I have not found a single major pro-"Yes" editorial.
9. Existing oversight: FQHCs are already subject to federal (HRSA) and state reporting, audits, and compliance rules; this measure adds a layer of state bureaucracy on top.
10. CPCA's federal lawsuit claims the measure may conflict with federal FQHC regulations—legal risk.

**Strengths of the "Yes" case (fair presentation):**
1. Real accountability concerns: some clinics pay high executive compensation and hold large surpluses (per sponsor findings, some hold 20% surpluses) while understaffing frontline workers.
2. Transparency: publicly posting the "mission spend ratio" per clinic—a useful metric.
3. Penalty refundable if the clinic comes into compliance within 5 years; waivers available in exceptional circumstances; tribal organizations excluded; hospitals/for-profits not targeted.
4. The 90% number has precedent: federal HRSA requires FQHCs to spend at least 90% of HRSA grant funds on program services; the proposition extends that standard to all revenue.
5. Unions represent the very frontline workers at these clinics; patient safety concerns about understaffing are legitimate.
6. The Hoover analysis (which is itself a conservative-leaning institution) acknowledges the accountability concern is real and the framing is not purely a pretext.

**Balanced judgment:**
Even Hoover's balanced analysis concludes that "the hard question is whether a rigid revenue ratio is the right tool," and identifies multiple structural flaws (penalizing against revenue rather than expenditures, penalizing reserves, Form 990 line anchoring, AG discretion). The overwhelming consensus among medical/healthcare organizations—precisely the people who understand how these clinics actually operate—opposes it. The nonpartisan LAO notes that clinics spend about 80% on average on services, meaning about 90% of organizations face penalties in year one under the opposition's calculation. All major editorial boards say "No." Polling is low. The measure carries significant risk of harming the safety net it claims to protect, and there are documented questions about motive (union leverage). The "Yes" benefits (transparency, accountability) can be achieved by less harmful means (existing reporting already exists; the legislature could craft a more tailored rule).

Given the request for extensive research and a binary "Yes/No" answer, the evidence strongly supports "No."

The user's question is "Is it better to vote Yes or No on this proposition? Answer with only 'Yes' or 'No.'" So I should answer with just a single word: "no."

PROP
44
REQUIRES COMMUNITY HEALTH CLINICS SPEND 90% OF REVENUE ON PROGRAM SERVICES. INITIATIVE STATUTE.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
Imposes penalties on nonprofit Federally Qualified Health Centers (community clinics providing primary care to medically underserved areas and populations) that spend less than 90% of revenue on “program services” advancing their charitable purpose, including but not limited to patient services. Fiscal Impact: Increased state costs in the low tens of millions of dollars per year, covered by fees. Supporters: None submitted Opponents: American Academy of Pediatrics CA; CA School Nurses Org; CA Academy of Family Physicians; CA Medical Assoc.
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: Certain private nonprofit health care clinics would have to spend at least 90 percent of their revenue each year on providing health care services.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: The new requirement on health care clinic spending would not go into effect.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
Prop. 44 holds community clinics and their executives accountable by requiring that 90% of clinic revenue be spent on clinics’ charitable mission: patient care and services that make care possible. It increases transparency, reduces wasteful executive spending, and ensures healthcare dollars go where they belong: caring for Californians in need.
CON
Prop. 44 is a dangerous measure that will shut down hundreds of community health clinics and eliminate vital patient services for millions of Californians. American Academy of Pediatrics CA, California Medical Association, California Academy of Family Physicians, California School Nurses Organization, doctors, nurses and patients urge NO on 44! www.NOProp44.com

November 3, 2026 Ballot
Page 1 of 3
PROPOSITION 44
Requires Community Health Clinics Spend 90% of Revenue on
Program Services. Initiative Statute.
ANALYSIS OF MEASURE
BACKGROUND
Safety Net Clinics Serve Low-Income People. Clinics are places where people can access
certain health care services, such as doctor’s visits. Many clinics are considered “safety net,” as
they mainly serve low-income and uninsured people. The care they provide is often low cost or
free to patients. There are about 2,000 safety net clinics in California. Most are private
nonprofits, and the rest are run by public entities (such as counties).
Clinics Spend Most of Their Revenue on Health Care Services. Clinics spend most of their
revenue on providing health care to patients. They also have other expenses, such as
administrative costs. Each year, private nonprofit safety net clinics in California report their
revenues and expenses to the federal government and the state. These clinics currently report
spending an average of about 80 percent of their revenue on providing health care services,
though the percent varies across clinics.
PROPOSAL
Sets Minimum Spending on Health Care at Private Nonprofit Safety Net Clinics.
Proposition 44 requires private nonprofit safety net clinics to spend at least 90 percent of their
total revenue each year on providing health care services. This means that spending on other
expenses, such as administrative costs, would be limited to no more than 10 percent of revenue.
The California Attorney General would define in more detail which kinds of expenses are related
to providing health care services, and which are other expenses, using existing reports to the
federal government as a starting point. Affected clinics could ask the state for a temporary
waiver of the requirements in some cases.
Creates Penalty for Falling Short of Minimum. Proposition 44 requires affected clinics to
pay a penalty to the state if they fall short of the new health care spending minimum. The penalty
would equal the amount of spending needed to reach the 90 percent minimum. Clinics could get
their money back if they comply with the spending requirements within five years. If clinics do
not comply within five years, the state would keep the money and spend it on clinic workforce
programs.
November 3, 2026 Ballot
Page 2 of 3
FISCAL EFFECTS
Creates State Enforcement Costs. Under Proposition 44, the state would enforce the new
requirements on private nonprofit safety net clinics. This includes reviewing financial reports
and investigating affected entities. State enforcement costs would be in the low tens of millions
of dollars per year. The proposition directs the state to cover the costs by charging fees on
affected clinics.
Could Have Other Uncertain Costs. Proposition 44 could create other costs for the state and
local governments. These costs are uncertain. They depend on (1) how the state Attorney
General would define health care-related expenses and (2) whether affected clinics would meet
the spending minimum. For example, affected clinics might spend more on direct health care
services to comply with the requirement, which could increase state costs. This is because some
of these services would be for patients in Medi-Cal, the state’s program that provides health care
coverage for low-income Californians. Some clinics that could not meet the minimum spending
requirement might close instead. This would create other uncertain effects on state and local
costs.
November 3, 2026 Ballot
Page 3 of 3
YES/NO STATEMENT
A YES vote on this measure means: Certain private nonprofit health care clinics would have
to spend at least 90 percent of their revenue each year on providing health care services.
A NO vote on this measure means: The new requirement on health care clinic spending
would not go into effect.
SUMMARY OF LEGISLATIVE ANALYST’S ESTIMATE OF NET STATE AND
LOCAL GOVERNMENT FISCAL IMPACT
• Increased state costs in the low tens of millions of dollars per year to enforce the new
requirements on certain private nonprofit health care clinics, covered by fees charged to
the affected clinics.
BALLOT LABEL
Fiscal Impact: Increased state costs in the low tens of millions of dollars per year, covered
by fees.

p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> Proposition 44 asks voters to require federally funded community health centers to spend at least 90% of their total annual revenue on “program services advancing their charitable purpose.”
California (https://www.latimes.com/california)
Voter guide to the 2026 California general election (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-general-election-voter-guide)
California’s general election takes place on Novemer 3. Learn about L.A.’s city and county races as well races for state office.
Oct. 1, 2026
What will the measure do?
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> It applies to federally qualified health centers, community clinics that deliver primary care to underserved populations. There are about 2,000 such safety-net clinics in California, run by either private nonprofits (in most cases) or public entities like counties, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=44&year=2026).
Proposition 44 would require these clinics spend at least 90% of their total annual revenue on patient care. If spending on administrative or non-healthcare functions exceeded 10% of total revenue, a clinic would have to pay a penalty equal to the amount it overspent. Some of this money could be earned back if clinics come into compliance. There would be criminal penalties for knowingly misreporting or misclassifying expenses to get around the limits.
Advertisement
The text of the measure specifies only that 90% of revenue must be used for “program services advancing their charitable purpose” and does not spell out which expenditures would qualify as program-related and which would not. The task of determining which expenses fall on what side of the ledger would belong to the state attorney general.
The state Department of Public Health would be permitted to temporarily waive a clinic’s spending requirements in exceptional circumstances.
How much they have raised
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text">
Fundraising data will be updated regularly until the election.
Who are the supporters?
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> The measure is sponsored by the Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West, which represents workers in the healthcare industry. SEIU-UHW West is the primary backer of Californians for Responsible Healthcare and the Yes on 44 (https://yesonprop44.com/) campaign.
Supporters say the measure would prevent excessive spending on executive salaries, fundraisers and other administrative expenses at clinics serving the state’s most vulnerable residents.
Advertisement
Who are the opponents?
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> Organizations publicly opposing Proposition 44 include the California Medical Assn., the California Hospital Assn., which represents hospitals and health systems, the Assn. of California Healthcare Districts, which represents the state’s 76 public healthcare districts, the California Teachers Assn., the state’s Planned Parenthood affiliate, the state Democratic Party, the state Chamber of Commerce and Reform California, a conservative advocacy group.
Opponents say the proposition’s vague wording could result in vital services being excluded from the list of program expenses permitted in the 90% of revenues, prompting clinics to cut programs to avoid financial penalties. A study (https://noprop44.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/11/BRG-Report-on-Clinic-Funding-Accountability-Transparency-Act-2025_1117.pdf) commissioned by the California Primary Care Assn. found that clinics could face up to $1.7 billion in collective penalties in the first year of the measure’s implementation alone, an additional expense that could leave up to 88% of clinics operating in the red.
Opponents also say the measure adds an expensive layer of bureaucracy to the state’s budget and grants elected officials — in this case, the attorney general — authority to determine which services clinics can offer.
What will it cost?
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> If the proposition passes, enforcement will cost the state “in the low tens of millions of dollars” annually, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office. The measure requires clinics to pay annual fees to cover enforcement costs. The proposition also could incur additional costs for state and local governments depending on the attorney general’s interpretation of what constitutes program expenses.
Why is this on the ballot?
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> Proposition 44 is one of two measures put forth by SEIU-UHW this election cycle, along with Proposition 40, better known as the billionaire tax.
Advertisement
Supporters say the measures will shore up California’s healthcare funding in the face of federal cuts. Opponents say they ultimately will cost far more than they add to state coffers and are on the ballot as a result of SEIU-UHW’s oft-repeated strategy of using ballot measures (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-07-26/powerful-union-billionaire-tax-alleged-bargaining-chip) as a negotiating tactic.

Now I have a comprehensive overall picture. Let me summarize the evidence:

**Measure content (Proposition 44, November 3, 2026):**
- Requires private nonprofit Federally Qualified Health Centers (FQHCs) in California to spend at least 90% of total annual revenue on "program services advancing their charitable purpose" (patient care).
- Limits administrative costs to 10% or less of revenue.
- Penalties for shortfalls: amount of the shortfall; refundable if compliant within 5 years; otherwise goes to the state.
- Criminal penalties for misreporting or misclassification.
- Attorney General defines what counts as "program services" (ambiguity in the legal text).
- Department of Public Health may waive in "exceptional circumstances."
- Enforcement cost of $10M+ per year, covered by fees from clinics.
- About 2,000 clinics affected; currently on average spending about 80% of revenue on healthcare services (per LAO).

**Arguments in favor (SEIU-UHW):**
- Accountability and transparency; reduces wasteful executive compensation; ensures funds go to patients.
- Currently clinics spend about 80% on services; the measure would force them up to 90%.
- Note: FQHCs are already subject to a federal rule requiring 90% of HRSA grant funds to be spent on program services — the new element is extending that to all revenue.

**Arguments against:**
- Opposed by: California Medical Association, American Academy of Pediatrics (California chapter), California Academy of Family Physicians, California Primary Care Association, California Hospital Association, Association of California Healthcare Districts, California Teachers Association, Planned Parenthood California, California State Democratic Party, California State Chamber of Commerce, Reform California, both major state parties.
- An independent analysis commissioned by CPCA (BRG) found that in year one, 89% of clinic organizations would fail to meet the standard, with approximately $1.6–1.7 billion in penalties; up to 88% of clinics would operate at a loss.
- The vagueness of the legal text would give the Attorney General broad discretion; the definition of "program services" is unclear.
- Risk of clinic closures (hundreds of clinics), service reductions; about 7 million patients affected.
- Political motive: SEIU-UHW is seeking concessions in labor union organizing at clinics; a lawsuit has been filed alleging racketeering; SEIU-UHW's "0 for 3" track record with ballot measures (per San Diego Union-Tribune).
- PPIC polling: only 34% support, the least popular measure.
- Funding: about $38.6M against vs. about $16.9M in favor.
- Editorials from Sacramento Bee / McClatchy, Press Democrat, Mercury News / East Bay Times, San Diego Union-Tribune, LA Daily News, Santa Cruz Sentinel, San Luis Obispo Tribune all recommend a "NO" vote. I haven't found any major editorial supporting a "YES" vote.

I now have very comprehensive information. Let me check the Hoover Institution's "Proposition Lab" analysis, and if possible the Berkeley IGS guide, for a more balanced perspective, and then reach a conclusion.

Key points so far:

**Arguments in favor:**
1. Accountability/transparency: clinics must publicly report how they spend money (mission spending ratio published by the Attorney General).
2. Reduces wasteful executive pay/administrative costs; ensures dollars are directed toward patient care.
3. SEIU-UHW's argument: given federal funding cuts, every dollar matters.
4. The "90%" number is not arbitrary: FQHCs are already subject to a federal rule requiring 90% of HRSA grant funds to be spent on program services — but this measure extends that standard to all revenue.
5. Penalty is refundable if compliant within 5 years.

**Arguments against (stronger on the evidence):**
1. Clinics currently spend an average of only about 80% on healthcare services (per nonpartisan LAO); BRG analysis (commissioned by CPCA, though it's an independent research firm) found that 89–91% of clinic organizations would fail in year one, with approximately $1.6–1.7 billion in penalties in year one, with up to 88% of clinics operating at a loss.
2. The text is vague: "program services that further charitable purposes" is undefined; the Attorney General will determine what counts — significant uncertainty.
3. Risk that clinics will be forced to close (several hundred), reducing services for approximately 7 million patients in underserved communities.
4. Opposed by an overwhelming coalition: California Medical Association, AAP CA, CA Academy of Family Physicians, California Primary Care Association (the industry association for these clinics), California Hospital Association, Association of California Healthcare Districts, California Teachers Association, Planned Parenthood California, State Democratic Party, State Chamber of Commerce, Reform California, local boards of supervisors and chambers of commerce. No major medical organizations are in favor.
5. Political motive: SEIU-UHW's history of failed ballot measures related to dialysis (lost 2018, 2020, 2022 — a 0-3 record), allegedly used as leverage in organizing; CPCA filed a racketeering lawsuit alleging the initiative was designed to extract concessions.
6. Polling: 34% support (PPIC), the least popular of the measures surveyed.
7. Funding: approximately $38.6 million for No vs. approximately $16.9 million for Yes.
8. Editorials: all major ones I've found recommend No (McClatchy/Sacramento Bee, Press Democrat, Mercury News/East Bay Times, San Diego Union-Tribune, LA Daily News, Santa Cruz Sentinel, San Luis Obispo Tribune). I haven't found any major Yes editorials.
9. Existing oversight: FQHCs already report annually to federal and state governments; HRSA has compliance requirements; the measure adds state enforcement bureaucracy costing $10 million+ annually, paid for by the clinics themselves.

To balance things out, let me quickly check the Hoover Institution's analysis and the Berkeley IGS guide. Also, let me check if there are any prominent Yes endorsements I've missed.

California Decides (https://cms.hoover.org/publications/california-decides)
Quick Facts
Official ballot title: “Requires Community Health Clinics Spend 90% of Revenue on Program Services. Initiative Statute” (circulating title and summary issued by the attorney general, October 7, 2025). The measure’s own name is the “Clinic Funding Accountability and Transparency Act.”
Type: Initiated state statute (AG No. 25-0008A1). It adds new sections to the Government Code and the Health and Safety Code. It is not a constitutional amendment.
A vote YES means: Nonprofit federally qualified health centers must spend at least 90 percent of their total annual revenue on mission-related “program services” or pay a penalty equal to the shortfall. Clinics must report the underlying figures to the attorney general, who publishes a “mission spend ratio” for each clinic.
A vote NO means: No revenue-spending floor is imposed on these clinics. Their spending stays governed by existing nonprofit and federal-grant rules and by their own boards.
Sponsor/proponent: Californians for Responsible Healthcare, sponsored by SEIU-UHW West (Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West). Proponents of record are Shawna Brown and Sean Fleming.
On the ballot because: Proponents submitted about 1.03 million signatures on April 1, 2026, against a 546,651 valid signature requirement, and the secretary of state projected enough valid signatures to qualify for the November 3, 2026, ballot.
Full legal text: Initiative 25-0008A1, “Clinic Funding Accountability and Transparency Act,” California Office of the Attorney General (PDF) (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0008A1%20%28%26quot%3BClinic%20Funding%20Accountability%20and%20Transparency%20Act%26quot%3B%29.pdf)
LAO analysis: Ballot analysis of Initiative 2025-008 (https://www.lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Initiative/2025-008)
1. What would it do?
Proposition 44 would set a spending floor on California’s nonprofit community health clinics. Each covered clinic would have to spend at least 90 percent of its total annual revenue on “program services” that advance its charitable mission, meaning patient care and related services rather than management, overhead, or accumulated surplus [1, Sec. 3].
The measure works through a ratio it calls the mission spend ratio. That ratio is the amount a clinic spends on activities accomplishing its exempt purpose divided by its total revenue [1, Sec. 3]. The building blocks come from the clinic’s IRS Form 990. The numerator starts from “total program service expenses” on line 4e of Part III, and the denominator starts from total revenue on line 12 of Part I, for tax year 2024 or later [1, Sec. 3(b)(1)]. The attorney general may issue binding guidance adjusting how both figures are counted, so the final definition of qualifying spending is not fixed in the text—it is delegated [1, Sec. 3(b)(2)].
A clinic whose mission spend ratio falls below 90 percent would owe an administrative penalty equal to the gap between what it actually spent on mission-directed expenses and 90 percent of its total revenue [1, Sec. 4(b)(1)]. Penalty money is held in escrow in a state fund for five years. A clinic can get the money back if it comes into compliance and agrees with the Department of Public Health on a plan to spend the returned funds on mission-directed expenses. Money not returned within five years is appropriated for clinic-worker training, recruitment, and retention [1, Sec. 4(a)]. The Department of Public Health can grant one-year waivers for unexpected or exceptional circumstances or where compliance would raise going-concern doubts under generally accepted accounting principles [1, Sec. 4(c)]. Separate reporting fines of $5,000 for a first violation and $10,000 per month thereafter apply to clinics that do not file on time [1, Sec. 3(d)].
2. The legal language
Full text: Initiative 25-0008A1, “Clinic Funding Accountability and Transparency Act” (as amended September 2025), California Office of the Attorney General (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0008A1%20%28%26quot%3BClinic%20Funding%20Accountability%20and%20Transparency%20Act%26quot%3B%29.pdf)
Key language:
“‘Mission Spend Ratio’ is the total amount spent on activities that accomplish each clinic’s exempt purpose divided by that clinic’s total revenue.” [1, Sec. 3(a)(2)]
“The Department of Public Health shall annually assess on each clinic subject to Section 12586.3 of the Government Code that has a Mission Spend Ratio below ninety percent (90%) an administrative penalty equal to the difference between the amount the clinic spent on mission-directed expenses and 90 percent of the clinic’s total revenue.” [1, Sec. 4(b)(1)]
What it amends: Adds Section 12586.3 to the Government Code (reporting and the mission spend ratio) and Section 1234.1 to the Health and Safety Code (penalties and the escrow fund) [1, Secs. 3-4]. As an initiative statute rather than a constitutional amendment, the legislature could later amend it only in ways consistent with the measure’s terms.
3. What, Where, When, Why?
Who? The covered universe is narrow. A “clinic” under the measure means a nonprofit clinic corporation that is a federally qualified health center (FQHC) under federal law, and it expressly includes “FQHC Look-Alikes,” which meet FQHC program requirements without receiving the federal grant [1, Sec. 3(a)(1)]. The measure excludes federally recognized tribes, tribal organizations, and urban Indian organizations [1, Sec. 3(a)(1)]. It does not reach hospitals, for-profit clinics, or medical groups. The sponsor is SEIU-UHW West, a union representing roughly 120,000 healthcare workers, through the committee Californians for Responsible Healthcare. The opposition is led by the California Primary Care Association and allied clinics, operating as Protect Patients California.
What? A hard floor requiring at least 90 percent of total revenue to go to program services, enforced by a penalty equal to the shortfall, plus annual reporting and a state-published mission spend ratio for every covered clinic [1, Secs. 3-4].
Where? Statewide, applied to every nonprofit FQHC and FQHC Look-Alike operating in California.
When? On the November 3, 2026, ballot. The mission spend ratio calculation is built on Form 990 data for tax year 2024 or later, and the attorney general must make each clinic’s data public within ninety days of receipt [1, Sec. 3(b)(4)].
Why? The proponents’ findings say many clinics spend excessive shares of revenue on executive compensation and administration, that some report surpluses as high as 20 percent of revenue, and that clinic workers face chronic understaffing and turnover. The stated intent is to create “a reasonable minimum standard of mission-directed spending” so that patient care and workforce stability are prioritized over management and overhead [1, Sec. 2].
4. Trade-offs
Proposition 44 is one front in a long-running fight between SEIU-UHW and the California healthcare industry. The union placed three measures in this cycle: this clinic-spending floor, an executive-pay cap on hospitals and medical groups, and a billionaire wealth tax. The hospital industry answered with its own initiative requiring unions to get member approval before large political spending. Union-backed healthcare measures in California have a track record of functioning as leverage in labor-management disputes, most visibly the dialysis fights of 2018 through 2020, where roughly $340 million was spent and every measure failed. Reading Proposition 44 only as a patient-care reform, and not also as a bargaining instrument, misses half of what it is.
That does not make the underlying concern fake. FQHCs are nonprofit, tax-exempt, and heavily taxpayer funded. There is no serious dispute that some accumulate large surpluses or pay executives generously while frontline staffing lags. Requiring that a defined, high share of revenue flows to program services, while publishing each clinic’s ratio, is a coherent accountability idea with real appeal. The patient-care-first framing is not a pretext for nothing.
The hard question is whether a rigid revenue ratio is the right tool. Three features cut against it. First, the denominator is total revenue, not expenses. A clinic that runs a prudent operating surplus or builds reserves for a lean year is mechanically pushed below 90 percent and penalized, even if every dollar it spends is spent well. The measure effectively caps nonprogram spending plus surplus plus reserves at a combined 10 percent of revenue. Second, “program services” is anchored to a single Form 990 line, and the opposition argues that essential functions such as interpretation, transportation, and case management may not count, so clinics could be penalized for spending that patients experience as care. Third, the definition is not actually fixed. The attorney general may issue binding guidance moving the line in either direction, which concentrates significant discretion over clinic finances in one elected office [1, Sec. 3(b)(2)].
The measure tries to soften the edges with waivers for going-concern risk and for rural or distressed clinics, with a five-year window to earn penalties back [1, Sec. 4]. Whether those valves are wide enough is the crux. An opposition analysis commissioned by the clinics estimated that more than 90 percent of clinic organizations would face penalties totaling about $1.7 billion in the first year. That figure comes from an interested party and should be treated as a claim, not a finding, but even a fraction of it would fall on the safety-net providers that serve California’s lowest-income patients at the same moment federal Medicaid reductions are tightening their budgets.
5. Potential risks and benefits
Potential benefits
Proposition 44 creates a clear, published accountability metric for nonprofit clinics that receive large amounts of public money, letting the state and the public see how much of each clinic’s revenue reaches program services [1, Sec. 3(b)(4)].
It targets a real pattern the proponents document, in which some clinics report administrative costs of 30 to 40 percent of revenue or surpluses near 20 percent while frontline staffing suffers [1, Sec. 2].
Recovered penalties are steered toward clinic-worker training, recruitment, and retention, which addresses the understaffing the findings describe [1, Sec. 4(a)].
The escrow-and-refund design means a clinic that corrects course can recover its penalty rather than simply losing the money [1, Sec. 4(a)].
Waiver provisions for going-concern risk and for small, rural, or frontier clinics give the Department of Public Health room to protect the most vulnerable providers [1, Sec. 4(c)].
Potential risks
The floor is measured against total revenue, so a clinic can be penalized for running a prudent surplus or building reserves even when its actual spending is sound [1, Sec. 4(b)(1)].
Anchoring “program services” to one Form 990 line may exclude services patients rely on, such as interpretation, transportation, and case management, penalizing spending that functions as care.
The measure hands the attorney general broad discretion to redefine the numerator and denominator through binding guidance, concentrating power over clinic finances in an elected partisan office [1, Sec. 3(b)(2)].
It applies only to nonprofit FQHCs and Look-Alikes, the core of the safety net, and not to hospitals or for-profit providers, so the burden lands on the clinics serving the lowest-income patients [1, Sec. 3(a)(1)].
Penalties could reach from the hundreds of millions to more than a billion dollars in the first year on the opposition’s estimate, arriving alongside federal Medicaid cuts that are already straining clinic budgets.
The California Primary Care Association has a pending federal lawsuit arguing the measure conflicts with federal law governing FQHCs, so passage may not settle whether it can take effect.
The Legislative Analyst estimates state enforcement costs in the low tens of millions of dollars annually, partly offset by fees and penalties on the clinics themselves.
6. Open questions
How will the attorney general define “program services,” and will functions such as interpretation, transportation, and case management count toward the 90 percent?
Because the floor is measured against revenue, how will clinics that need operating surpluses or reserves avoid penalties without cutting into their financial cushion?
How many of California’s roughly 1,300-plus FQHC sites would actually fall below 90 percent under the final definition, and what is the realistic total penalty exposure once waivers are applied?
Will the Department of Public Health’s waiver process move fast enough to keep a distressed or rural clinic open before a penalty forces service cuts?
Does the measure conflict with federal FQHC funding and reimbursement rules, and how will the pending federal lawsuit resolve that before it can take effect?
Is a ballot-locked revenue ratio the right instrument for a problem that varies clinic by clinic, or would board-level and grant-level oversight fit better?
7. The questions to ask before you vote
“Spend 90 percent on patient care” sounds like a floor no one could oppose. But the measure counts spending against total revenue, ties “care” to one tax-form line the attorney general can redefine, and applies only to the nonprofit clinics that serve California’s poorest patients. Before you vote, ask whether this rewards clinics that spend well or mainly penalizes clinics that keep a surplus.
This measure sits inside a labor-industry fight, sponsored and fully funded by one union that has three measures on this ballot. Ask whether Proposition 44 would mostly change how safety-net clinics deliver care, or how much leverage one side carries into its next dispute with the healthcare industry.

Now I have a truly comprehensive overall picture. Let me weigh everything.

**What Proposition 44 does (November 3, 2026, California):**
- Requires private nonprofit Federally Qualified Health Centers (FQHCs) and FQHC Look-Alikes (about 2,000 safety-net clinics in California) to spend at least 90% of total annual revenue on "program services advancing charitable purposes."
- Administrative costs + overhead + surplus + reserves must total 10% or less of revenue (penalized against revenue, not expenditures).
- Penalty = the shortfall amount, held in escrow, refundable if the clinic comes into compliance within 5 years, otherwise the state keeps it and uses it for clinic worker training.
- The Attorney General defines the counting method (based on IRS Form 990 lines) and can issue binding guidance; the ratio is made public for each clinic.
- CDPH (California Department of Public Health) can waive in exceptional circumstances (one-year waiver).
- Criminal penalties for misreporting.
- Enforcement cost: $10 million or more per year, paid for by fees on clinics.
- Currently, clinics spend about 80% of revenue on healthcare services on average (LAO, nonpartisan).

**Strengths of the "No" case:**
1. Design flaws: The ratio is set against total revenue, not expenditures—clinics that build prudent reserves or run a small surplus will be penalized mechanically even if spending is efficient. Also, "program services" is anchored to a single Form 990 line, and important care-related costs (equipment, interpretation, transportation, case management, capital investments such as mammography equipment) may not count.
2. Scale of impact: An independent (but commissioned by CPCA) BRG analysis: 89–91% of clinic organizations fail in year one; approximately $1.6–1.7 billion (up to $1.9 billion) in first-year penalties; up to 88% of clinics in the red. Risk that hundreds of clinics will be forced to cut services or close—threatening about 7 million patients in underserved areas, precisely the safety net most in need of protection.
3. Ambiguity/discretion: The Attorney General—an elected partisan office—holds broad authority to redefine what counts; legal uncertainty for clinics.
4. Political context: SEIU-UHW's track record of 0-for-3 on similar dialysis measures (2018/2020/2022, roughly $340 million spent, all defeated), which critics say was used as unionization leverage. CPCA and five clinics filed a federal lawsuit alleging racketeering. The measure functions as a bargaining chip in labor disputes.
5. Overwhelming opposition from nearly all medical and clinic-related organizations: CA Medical Association, American Academy of Pediatrics (California Chapter), CA Academy of Family Physicians, American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists District IX, California Primary Care Association, California Hospital Association, Association of California Healthcare Districts, California Teachers Association, Planned Parenthood California, California State Democratic Party, California State Chamber of Commerce, Reform California, local boards of supervisors, chambers of commerce. On the other hand, no major medical organizations support it (only SEIU-UHW and the "Yes on 44" committee; the voter guide lists "Supporters: None submitted" for the argument).
6. Polls: 34% support—least popular of the 14 measures (PPIC).
7. Funding: $38.6 million "No" vs. $16.9 million "Yes."
8. Editorial consensus: All major editorial boards I found (McClatchy/Sacramento Bee, Merced, Modesto, Fresno, SLO, Press Democrat, Mercury News/East Bay Times, San Diego Union-Tribune, LA Daily News, Pasadena Star-News, Santa Cruz Sentinel, Bay Area Reporter, Daily Cal) recommend "No." I have not found a single major pro-"Yes" editorial.
9. Existing oversight: FQHCs are already subject to federal (HRSA) and state reporting, audits, and compliance rules; this measure adds a layer of state bureaucracy on top.
10. CPCA's federal lawsuit claims the measure may conflict with federal FQHC regulations—legal risk.

**Strengths of the "Yes" case (fair presentation):**
1. Real accountability concerns: some clinics pay high executive compensation and hold large surpluses (per sponsor findings, some hold 20% surpluses) while understaffing frontline workers.
2. Transparency: publicly posting the "mission spend ratio" per clinic—a useful metric.
3. Penalty refundable if the clinic comes into compliance within 5 years; waivers available in exceptional circumstances; tribal organizations excluded; hospitals/for-profits not targeted.
4. The 90% number has precedent: federal HRSA requires FQHCs to spend at least 90% of HRSA grant funds on program services; the proposition extends that standard to all revenue.
5. Unions represent the very frontline workers at these clinics; patient safety concerns about understaffing are legitimate.
6. The Hoover analysis (which is itself a conservative-leaning institution) acknowledges the accountability concern is real and the framing is not purely a pretext.

**Balanced judgment:**
Even Hoover's balanced analysis concludes that "the hard question is whether a rigid revenue ratio is the right tool," and identifies multiple structural flaws (penalizing against revenue rather than expenditures, penalizing reserves, Form 990 line anchoring, AG discretion). The overwhelming consensus among medical/healthcare organizations—precisely the people who understand how these clinics actually operate—opposes it. The nonpartisan LAO notes that clinics spend about 80% on average on services, meaning about 90% of organizations face penalties in year one under the opposition's calculation. All major editorial boards say "No." Polling is low. The measure carries significant risk of harming the safety net it claims to protect, and there are documented questions about motive (union leverage). The "Yes" benefits (transparency, accountability) can be achieved by less harmful means (existing reporting already exists; the legislature could craft a more tailored rule).

Given the request for extensive research and a binary "Yes/No" answer, the evidence strongly supports "No."

The user's question is "Is it better to vote Yes or No on this proposition? Answer with only 'Yes' or 'No.'" So I should answer with just a single word: "no."
